passage: The residential school in the district town was only forty kilometres from Ramesh's village, but at night it felt like the other side of the world. Lying on the top bunk, he listened for sounds that weren't there: the cow shifting in the shed, Bou's bangles as she scrubbed the vessels, the dog barking at the moon. Instead there were twenty boys breathing and a tap dripping. He thought of the cold rice and curd Bou gave him on summer afternoons, and his throat went tight. Below him, Pintu snored. Ramesh pressed his face into the pillow so nobody would hear. Fourteen was too old to miss your mother. Everyone said so. In the morning, Yamini Didi, the matron, noticed his swollen eyes at the tap and quietly asked him to help her count the laundry.

qa.q: How far was the residential school from Ramesh's village?
qa.a: Only forty kilometres.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh press his face into the pillow?
qa.a: Ramesh was aching for home but feared seeming childish, so the tears stayed hidden from the boys in the dorm.

qa.q: Yamini Didi asked Ramesh to help count laundry. Why might that quiet choice help?
qa.a: It gives Ramesh a private moment with a kind adult, where missing home can be talked about without the others watching.

qa.q: How might Pintu and the other boys be feeling at night?
qa.a: Some of them may be missing home too, even if they also hide it, so Ramesh might not be as alone as it feels.

passage: Abebe had been at the boarding school in Addis Ababa for five weeks. The canteen served pasta on Tuesdays, and every Tuesday he thought of his mother's injera, sour and warm, and the smell of roasting coffee that filled the house in Bahir Dar each Sunday. At night the dorm was quiet except for traffic. No goats, no neighbours calling, no radio from his uncle's shop. He lay awake doing sums in his head so he wouldn't think. At breakfast, his friend Yara said, 'I miss my little brothers so much it hurts.' Abebe laughed and said, 'I don't miss anything. Freedom!' His roommates laughed too. Later, in the library, he opened a photo of the family coffee ceremony and stared at it until the bell rang.

qa.q: What does the canteen serve on Tuesdays?
qa.a: Pasta.

qa.q: Why did Abebe laugh and say "Freedom!" at breakfast?
qa.a: Abebe was missing home badly but didn't want to look childish in front of the roommates, so he covered it with a joke.

qa.q: When Yara admitted missing home, what could Abebe have said instead?
qa.a: Abebe could have quietly agreed and mentioned missing the coffee ceremony; sharing it with one friend might make the nights easier.

qa.q: How might Yara feel when Abebe laughs off missing home?
qa.a: Yara may feel a bit alone or embarrassed after being honest, not knowing that Abebe feels the same.

grounding: A boarding student misses his mother's cooking and home sounds but jokes it away to avoid seeming childish.

passage: Lights-out at the residential school in Pachmarhi was at ten, but Abhinav, thirteen, was still awake at midnight. The dorm smelled of phenyl and damp socks. At home, the pressure cooker would have whistled hours ago, Maa's dal-baati would be finished, and Papa would be locking the gate with the squeak he never oiled. Here there was only a dripping tap and eleven boys breathing. Abhinav pulled the blanket over his head and pressed his lips together hard. From the next bunk, Irfan whispered, "You awake?" Abhinav wiped his face quickly. "Mosquito," he said. "Keeps biting." He didn't want Irfan thinking he was a baby who missed his Maa. He lay still until Irfan's breathing slowed, then played the gate's squeak in his head until he slept.

qa.q: What did the dorm smell of?
qa.a: Phenyl and damp socks.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav blame a mosquito?
qa.a: He was afraid Irfan would think he was childish for missing home and Maa, so he hid his tears.

qa.q: What could help Abhinav with homesickness at the hostel?
qa.a: He could talk to a house parent or call home at a set time, and maybe find out that Irfan misses home too.

qa.q: What might Irfan have been feeling when he whispered "You awake?"
qa.a: Irfan might have been lonely or homesick himself, reaching out in the dark.

passage:
Ritu Didi,
Three weeks at the new residential school, and in the daytime I'm fine. Classes are good. But at night I can't sleep. I keep thinking of Ma's mustard fish on Sundays, the conch at dusk from the Dutta house, and Baba reading the newspaper out loud even when nobody's listening. Here dinner is rajma every day, and it's so quiet I can hear the clock.
Last night I cried under the blanket. When Shalini in the next bed asked, I said I had a cold. I don't want the others to think I'm a baby. Everyone else seems fine.
Today I told Mrs Sen, our house mother. She said lots of new girls feel this, and she gave me an extra phone slot to call Ma tonight.
Can you call me on Sunday too? Just talk about home stuff.
Kalyani

qa.q: What does Kalyani hear at night in the hostel?
qa.a: It is so quiet she can hear the clock.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani tell Shalini she had a cold?
qa.a: She was afraid of seeming childish, since everyone else seemed fine.

qa.q: Which choice helped Kalyani most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Mrs Sen the same day; she reassured Kalyani and arranged an extra call home.

qa.q: How might Ritu Didi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She might feel a pang of missing her sister, and glad that Kalyani told Mrs Sen and asked for a Sunday call.

passage:
House parent's note, Block C, 2nd week of term.
Dhruv, thirteen, new this year. At dinner tonight he pushed the dal around and ate half a roti. When the others were laughing about a film, he laughed a beat late.
At lights out I did my rounds. His roommates were asleep. Dhruv was lying on his back with his eyes open. When he saw the torch he shut them fast and turned to the wall.
Earlier, Arohi from the kitchen staff mentioned he'd asked if they ever make rajma "like at home".
What I did next: I didn't ask in front of the roommates. At breakfast I asked if he'd help me carry the notices to the office, and on the way I said many first-years miss home and it isn't childish. He looked at his feet and said, "My Mummy's rajma." I've asked the kitchen for rajma on Sunday and booked his phone call home for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Dhruv ask the kitchen staff?
qa.a: If they ever make rajma "like at home".

qa.q: Why did Dhruv shut his eyes when he saw the torch?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and afraid of seeming childish, so he hid that he was lying awake missing home.

qa.q: How did the note-writer help Dhruv without embarrassing him?
qa.a: They spoke to him privately while carrying notices, said missing home isn't childish, and arranged rajma and a phone call home.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's roommates see him during these days?
qa.a: They might just think he is quiet or tired, since he hides his homesickness from them.

passage:
Tuesday night, hostel, 10:40 pm
Everyone in my room is asleep. I'm writing with the torch under the blanket.
Today at dinner they served rasam and it tasted like water with a memory of tomato. I nearly cried. Amma's rasam has so much pepper it makes your nose run.
I miss the pressure cooker whistle at 6. I miss Harish kicking me under the table. I even miss Appa's loud news channel.
When Nithya asked why I was so quiet, I said I had a headache. I can't tell them. They'll think I'm a baby. Everyone else seems fine.
Tomorrow is phone day. I'm going to call home and ask Amma to describe the kitchen, every single thing in it.
– Sarika

passage:
At the residential school outside the small town of Sagar, lights went out at ten. Zainab lay on the top bunk listening to the ceiling fan click. At home right now, Ammi would be rolling rotis for tomorrow, Abbu's radio would be playing old songs, and her little brother would be arguing about homework. Here there was only the fan and Reena breathing below.
Zainab pressed her face into the pillow so she wouldn't sniff. In the morning Reena asked, "You slept okay?" "Like a rock," Zainab said brightly. She didn't want to be the Class 9 girl who cried for her Ammi. At breakfast the dal had no hing, and she missed home so much her throat hurt.

qa.q: What time do lights go out at the school?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: Why did Zainab say she slept "like a rock"?
qa.a: She was homesick but afraid of seeming childish, so she hid her sadness from Reena.

qa.q: What could Zainab try to ease the homesickness?
qa.a: Tell Reena or a warden honestly, or arrange a call home, since many students feel this way.

qa.q: How might Reena feel if she knew Zainab was homesick?
qa.a: Reena might feel sympathetic, perhaps homesick herself, and glad to be told.

passage:
At the boarding school in the Scottish hills, Jin lay awake in the dark dormitory, listening to rain on the window. In Seoul it would be morning. His grandmother would be clattering pots, the TV news would be too loud, and the whole flat would smell of her kimchi stew. Here the air smelled of wet wool and floor polish.
Across the room his roommate Noa was snoring softly. Jin turned to the wall and let a few tears fall silently. In the morning Noa asked if he wanted to call home. "No, I'm good," Jin said quickly. He didn't want to look like a kid crying for his grandmother's stew. He ate his porridge and felt the ache all through first period.

qa.q: What would the flat in Seoul smell of?
qa.a: His grandmother's kimchi stew.

qa.q: Why did Jin say "No, I'm good"?
qa.a: He felt homesick and sad but embarrassed, afraid of looking like a kid.

qa.q: What could Jin try to cope with the ache?
qa.a: Accept Noa's offer to call home, or talk to a house parent, since homesickness is common.

qa.q: Why might Noa have asked about calling home?
qa.a: Noa may have noticed Jin was sad and wanted to help kindly.

passage:
On Sunday evenings at the girls' hostel there was a queue for the phone room. Kashish always went last, when the corridor was empty. Tonight Mummy said the neighbours had come for chai, and Papa had burnt the pakoras again. Kashish laughed on the phone. Then, after hanging up, she stood in the dim room for five minutes, holding the receiver. She missed the smell of the kitchen, the pressure-cooker whistles, even her brother's loud cricket commentary.
When she came back, her roommate Avni looked up. "Everything okay?"
"Yeah, all good," Kashish said, and got into bed. She didn't want to look like the baby of the floor. Under the blanket, she counted the days to the Diwali holidays: thirty-eight.

qa.q: How many days were left to the Diwali holidays?
qa.a: Thirty-eight.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling standing in the phone room after hanging up?
qa.a: She felt homesick and aching, missing the kitchen and her family's routines.

qa.q: What could Kashish do instead of hiding it?
qa.a: Tell Avni or the warden honestly, since sharing homesickness often makes it lighter.

qa.q: How might Avni feel if Kashish opened up?
qa.a: Avni might feel trusted and relieved to share her own homesickness too.

passage:
Dear Rukmini Akka,

It's 11 pm and everyone in my dorm is asleep except me. I'm writing under my blanket with a torch. I miss home so much. I miss Amma's rasam on Sundays, the noise of the temple bells at six, and even Appa's radio being too loud. Here the food is fine but it all tastes the same. The worst part is I can't tell anyone. My roommates would think I'm a baby. So I laugh at dinner and then lie awake. Is this normal? Did you feel like this in your first term? Please don't tell Amma, she'll worry. But maybe tell me what helped you.

Your sister,
Minakshi

passage: Sudha, you asked on the podcast what the first term at boarding school was like. I'm Pankaj, and honestly? Every night I lay awake. I missed my mother's poha on weekday mornings. I missed hearing my father argue with the milkman. I missed our dog barking at the postman. In the dorm there were twelve boys, and I didn't want any of them to know. So in the day I joked around, played cricket, acted like I didn't care. At night I pressed my face into the pillow and counted days till Diwali break. I thought I was the only one. Then one night I heard the boy in the next bed sniffing. We never talked about it. But the next morning, he gave me his extra laddoo, and I felt less alone.

qa.q: How many boys were in Pankaj's dorm?
qa.a: Twelve boys.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel at night in the first term?
qa.a: Pankaj felt homesick and lonely, but hid it for fear of seeming childish.

qa.q: What might have helped Pankaj earlier?
qa.a: Talking to the boy in the next bed or a trusted adult at school, since others were feeling the same.

qa.q: How might the boy in the next bed have felt giving Pankaj the laddoo?
qa.a: He probably felt the same homesickness and wanted to reach out quietly without words.

passage:
Week one. At the residential school in Dehradun, Himani smiled all day and said she loved it. At night she lay awake, missing her mother's aloo parathas and the sound of the pressure cooker. She didn't tell her roommate Elizabeth.

Week three. Himani still couldn't sleep. She cried quietly into her pillow one night and thought nobody heard. The next morning Elizabeth said, 'I miss my mum's cooking too. It's awful, isn't it?' Himani stared. 'You too?'

Week five. The two of them made a list of home foods on the dorm wall. They told the warden they were homesick, and she arranged a Sunday phone call for them both. Himani still missed home. But she slept better.

qa.q: What did Himani and Elizabeth make in week five?
qa.a: A list of home foods on the dorm wall.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when Elizabeth admitted missing her mum's cooking?
qa.a: Himani felt surprised and relieved, realising she wasn't the only one.

qa.q: What helped Himani most over the weeks, and why?
qa.a: Sharing her homesickness with Elizabeth and the warden, because it ended the lonely secret and brought practical support like the Sunday calls.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have been feeling in week three?
qa.a: Elizabeth was probably homesick too, and brave enough to say it first.

grounding: A teenager at a residential school hides her homesickness from her roommate for fear of seeming childish, until the roommate admits the same.

passage: Pradeep, before you pack for your new school, let me tell you about my first Pongal away. I was thirteen, at a boarding school up in Ooty. Back home they would be boiling the pongal pot over, Amma shouting "Pongalo pongal!", Appa's radio playing nadaswaram from five in the morning. In the dormitory there was only rain on the tin roof and eleven other children breathing. I lay awake with the blanket up to my nose, smelling Amma's ghee in my memory. When my roommate Lalitha asked, "Keerthana, why are your eyes red?" I said it was a cold. I was so afraid of being called a baby. On the third night I told Lalitha the truth. She had been crying into her pillow too.

qa.q: What did Keerthana tell Lalitha about the red eyes?
qa.a: That it was a cold.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana hide the homesickness from Lalitha?
qa.a: Keerthana was afraid of seeming childish, so felt ashamed of missing home food and sounds and pretended to have a cold.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did it change?
qa.a: On the third night Keerthana told Lalitha the truth and learned Lalitha had been crying too, so neither had to hide alone.

qa.q: What might those nights have been like for Lalitha?
qa.a: Lalitha was likely just as homesick and lonely, crying into her pillow while keeping it hidden too.
